scope: Manual review of supplied labels; no relabelling applied. Verification is limited to inspected examples.

mappings.evidence: Inspected examples have passage walls with two pairs of opposing orthogonal normal directions; additional faces reflect repeated or split walls.

One example has six labelled walls with three opposing normal pairs around a common through axis; the other has two groups of six with the same structure. This supports a six-sided passage rather than a triangular passage.

Both examples have two inclined walls meeting in a V-shaped profile, open at an exterior stock face, and extending across the full stock along a common axis (span 2). Consistent with a triangular through slot, rather than a closed six-sided passage.

Both examples have six side walls forming three opposing normal pairs around a common depth axis, plus a perpendicular bottom face: seven labelled faces in each example. This supports a blind six-sided pocket.
Both examples have four axis-aligned faces: two opposing side walls, a floor, and a blind end wall. The feature opens at an exterior stock boundary, consistent with a rectangular blind slot.
Both examples have an inclined planar face and a perpendicular end face at a stock corner, consistent with a triangular blind step. User corrected the earlier provisional chamfer interpretation.

Both examples have five labelled faces: four enclosing side walls in two opposing orthogonal pairs, plus a perpendicular bottom. Their openings lie inside a stock face, consistent with rectangular blind pockets.

Highlighted faces are single inclined edge strips, with normals having two equal-magnitude components (approximately 0.7071) and one zero component. Their bounding boxes span an original stock edge, consistent with 45-degree chamfers. First example contains two such faces; second contains one.

Both inspected examples show two opposing walls joined by a perpendicular floor, forming a U-shaped channel through the full stock width. Supports rectangular through slot. User confirmed the earlier suspected duplicate was confusion with a blind slot; KIV resolved.
Both examples have two perpendicular axis-aligned faces forming an L-shaped step cross-section at a stock corner, each extending along Z from -1 to 1. Consistent with rectangular through steps.

Each inspected feature has three faces: one axis-aligned wall spanning the stock and two inclined faces meeting along a central ridge. First example has two such groups; second has one. This supports the two-sided through-step shape rather than a single slanted through-step face.

Both examples have one inclined planar face and one axis-aligned wall, each extending along X from -1 to 1. The full-width extent and sloped surface support slanted through steps rather than rectangular blind steps.

Both examples have three enclosing side walls with normals in a common cross-sectional plane, plus a perpendicular bottom face. This supports a blind triangular pocket rather than an open triangular blind step.

Previously inspected both examples: each has three mutually perpendicular labelled faces forming a corner recess, with two open sides at the stock boundary. This supports a rectangular blind step rather than an inclined chamfer strip. Normals independently checked against sampled XYZ geometry.

First example has three enclosing side walls spanning X from -1 to 1; second has two groups of three enclosing walls spanning Z from -1 to 1. Supports triangular passages rather than open V-shaped through slots.
